questions.hint: Count only the atoms whose centers lie in the plane. Keep an area-based count separate from a volume-based count.
questions.explanation: Planar number density is the effective number of atom centers on a plane divided by its repeat area. Planar packing factor instead divides the area covered by the atom cross-sections by the plane area. Atoms centered above or below do not contribute to the on-plane count. Symmetry-equivalent planes have equal densities.

questions.hint: A slip system needs two pieces of information: an allowed plane and a direction lying inside it.
questions.explanation: Plastic slip moves dislocations along a direction in a slip plane. Dense atomic rows and densely packed planes often favor easy slip. FCC has four distinct {111} slip-plane orientations, each with three in-plane <110> directions, so 4 × 3 = 12 slip systems. The three-direction count is per slip plane, not the entire cubic direction family. BCC has dense slip rows but no truly close-packed plane.

questions.hint: A slip system needs two pieces of information: an allowed plane and a direction lying inside it.
questions.explanation: Plastic slip moves dislocations along a direction in a slip plane. Dense atomic rows and densely packed planes often favor easy slip. FCC has four distinct {111} slip-plane orientations, each with three in-plane <110> directions, so 4 × 3 = 12 slip systems. The three-direction count is per slip plane, not the entire cubic direction family. BCC has dense slip rows but no truly close-packed plane.

questions.hint: Separate the machine measurements from the geometry-normalized material quantities.
questions.explanation: A load cell measures force and an extensometer measures gauge-length extension. Engineering stress is σ = F/A₀ and engineering strain is ε = ΔL/L₀. Thus a force-extension curve becomes a stress-strain curve by dividing by original area and gauge length. Stress has units Pa = N/m²; strain is dimensionless. Tensile tests measure elastic and plastic responses.

questions.explanation: Ductile fracture is accompanied by appreciable plastic strain and often necking and microvoid growth/coalescence. Brittle fracture involves little plastic strain and can have flat or faceted surfaces and chevrons. Intergranular paths follow boundaries; transgranular paths cross grains. Ductile deformation can provide warning, but neither the number of pieces nor a visual description alone defines the fracture mechanism.
